passages.title: Documenting Indigenous Culture
passages.text:
Having spent several decades trying to eliminate the unself-conscious “colonial gaze” characteristic of so many early ethnographic films, visual anthropologists from the industrialized West who study indigenous cultures are presently struggling with an even more profound transformation of their discipline. Because inexpensive video equipment is now available throughout the world, many indigenous peoples who were once examined by the Western ethnographer’s camera have begun to document their own cultures. Reaction to this phenomenon within Western anthropological circles is sharply divided.

One faction, led by anthropologist James Weiner, sees the proliferation of video and television as the final assault of Western values on indigenous cultures. Weiner argues that the spread of video represents “a devaluation of the different,” culminating in the replacement of genuine historical, linguistic, social, and cultural difference with superficial difference among electronic images. He believes that video technologies inevitably purvey a Western ontology, one based on realism, immediacy, and self-expression. Thus, Weiner concludes, using video technology costs indigenous peoples the very cultural identity they seek to record. Moreover, he maintains that anthropologists who attribute a paramount truth value to these films simply because they are made by indigenous peoples are theoretically naive.

But Weiner’s opponents contend that his views betray a certain nostalgia for the idea of the “noble savage.” One such opponent, anthropologist Faye Ginsburg, concedes that no Western object that has entered cultural circulation since the fifteenth century has been neutral, but she considers it little more than boilerplate technological determinism to argue that using a video camera makes one unwittingly Western. Unlike Weiner, Ginsburg maintains that non-Western indigenous peoples can use Western media without adopting the conventions of Western culture. In fact, Ginsburg and many other anthropologists believe that video affords societies—especially oral ones—an invaluable opportunity to strengthen native languages and traditions threatened by Western exposure.

The Brazilian fieldwork of anthropologist Terence Turner, who studies the relationship between traditional Kayapo culture and Kayapo videotapes, lends credence to Ginsburg’s position. Primarily an oral society, the Kayapo use video to document both ceremonial performances and transactions with representatives of the Brazilian government (this latter use is intended to provide legally binding records of the transactions). In contrast to Weiner’s argument that video foists a Western ontology onto its users, Turner has found that the representations of Kayapo ceremonies, including everything from the camerawork to the editing, conform to the same principle of beauty embodied in the ceremonies themselves, one rooted in a complex pattern of repetition and sequential organization. The videos aesthetically mirror the ceremonies. The camera is not so at odds with Kayapo culture, it seems, that it transforms any Kayapo who uses it into a Westerner.

summaries.standard:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

The debate over indigenous peoples using video technology to document their cultures, and whether doing so changes or preserves their cultural identity.

**Framework**

Present Debate

**Main Point**

There is a major debate among anthropologists about whether the use of video technology by indigenous people undermines their cultural identity or helps preserve it, with evidence suggesting that indigenous communities can use such technology in culturally specific ways.
**The Most Valuable Sentences:** - "Reaction to this phenomenon within Western anthropological circles is sharply divided." (end of P1) - "In contrast to Weiner’s argument that video foists a Western ontology onto its users, Turner has found that the representations of Kayapo ceremonies, including everything from the camerawork to the editing, conform to the same principle of beauty embodied in the ceremonies themselves, one rooted in a complex pattern of repetition and sequential organization." (P4)

**P1: The New Phenomenon and Its Controversy**

Now that cheap video equipment is accessible, many indigenous communities are filming their own cultures, creating debate among Western anthropologists about what this means.

**P2: Weiner’s View—Threat to Cultural Identity**

Weiner thinks that using Western video technology inevitably pushes Western values on indigenous cultures, potentially causing those cultures to lose their uniqueness, and he criticizes those who take indigenous-made videos as inherently more truthful.

**P3: Ginsburg’s View—Empowerment and Preservation**

Ginsburg (and others) argues that using a Western tool does not mean adopting Western beliefs, and in fact, video can help preserve and strengthen indigenous traditions, especially in oral cultures.

**P4: Example—Kayapo Videos Defy “Westernization”**

Fieldwork with the Kayapo shows that their videos reflect unique cultural aesthetics, supporting the view that they are not just becoming “Western” by picking up a camera—instead, they adapt the technology to match their own culture.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately and completely summarizes the passage?

choices.text: Some anthropologists argue that the proliferation of video technology has been harmful to indigenous peoples because it encourages the adoption of a Western ontology based on immediacy and self-expression.
By making video technology available to indigenous peoples throughout the world, anthropologists have succeeded in eliminating the "colonial gaze" that many early ethnographic films exhibited.

Anthropologists are divided in their assessments of the impact of video technology on indigenous peoples, but there is some evidence that video technology is compatible with the preservation of indigenous cultures.

Some anthropologists argue that the proliferation of video technology has actually strengthened indigenous cultures threatened by Western influences, but the long-term impact of video technology on indigenous cultures is still unknown.

The Kayapo people's use of video technology validates the position of one faction in the debate in anthropological circles regarding the effect of the proliferation of Western video technology on indigenous cultures.

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, which one of the following most accurately describes Faye Ginsburg's stance toward the position attributed to James Weiner?

choices.text: fundamental rejection
reluctant censure
mild disapproval
diplomatic neutrality
supportive interest

questions.prompt: Which one of the following is most analogous to the Kayapo's use of video to document ceremonial performances, as that use is described in the last paragraph?

explanationBlocks.heading: Stem
explanationBlocks.body: "Most Analogous" indicates that this is an *Analogy* questions, and as is typical with these questions, we get a *Defined Target*: "the Kayapo's use of video to document ceremonial performances." That means we should *Research First*, then *Predict* by trying to describe what we just read abstractly, thinking about what qualities a situation would need in order to be analogous.

explanationBlocks.heading: Research
explanationBlocks.body: The Kayapo's use of video is introduced as an *example* that "lends credence to Ginsburg’s position." What position is that? We find it in the last lines of the preceding paragraph. Ginsburg thinks indigenous people "can use Western media without adopting the conventions of Western culture." How do the ceremony videos exemplify that? The rest of the last paragraph tells us that "the videos aesthetically mirror the ceremonies" by "conform[ing] to the same principle of beauty embodied in the ceremonies themselves, one rooted in a complex pattern of repetition and sequential organization."

explanationBlocks.heading: Predict
explanationBlocks.body:
What qualities should we expect to see in a situation analogous to the Kayapo's use of video?

- Culture A's use of something from Culture B.
- That use *doesn't* indicate that Culture A is adopting Culture B more broadly because they're using the thing in a way that is unique to Culture A.

choices.text: As various groups have emigrated to North America, they have brought their culinary traditions with them and thereby altered the culinary practices of North America.
choices.explanation: This is Culture A (groups emigrating to North America) bringing their traditions with them and altering Culture B (North American culinary practices). We want Culture A borrowing something from Culture B and using it in a unique way, without taking on too much of B's culture.

choices.text: In the 1940s, Latin American composers incorporated African American inspired jazz instrumentation and harmonies into their music but remained faithful to the traditions of Latin American music.
choices.explanation: Culture A (Latin American composers) incorporates something (jazz instrumentation and harmonies) from Culture B (African American musicians). But because they remain faithful to traditions of Latin American music, they're using that thing in a unique way and not adopting the broader cultural traditions of African American jazz musicians.

choices.text: Some writers are predicting that the interactive nature of the Internet will fundamentally reshape fiction, and they are already producing narratives that take advantage of this capacity.
choices.explanation: This answer doesn't give us two cultures in which one adopts something from the other.

choices.text: In the late 1980s, some fashion designers produced lines of various articles of clothing that imitated fashions that were current in the 1920s and 1930s.
choices.explanation: This answer gives us Culture A (1980's fashion designers) adopting from Culture B (1920's and 30's fashion), but it doesn't specify that 80's fashion didn't take on the whole look and feel of 20's and 30's fashion. Now, those of us who were alive in the 80's can use our real-world knowledge to fill in that missing piece of information. Late 80's was definitely not full flapper. But we're not allowed to fill in real world info like that. In order to be analogous, we'd need this answer to tell us explicitly that the 80's designers used these styles in a uniquely 80's way (shoulder pads and zoot suits, anyone?).

choices.text: Early in the twentieth century, some experimental European artists rejected the representational traditions of Western painting and began to produce works inspired by surrealist literature.
choices.explanation: Like D, this answer gives us Culture A (early 20th century experimental European artists) adopting from Culture B (surrealist literature), but it doesn't specify that Culture A did it in a unique way that didn't go full-surrealist.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, Weiner claims that an essential characteristic of Western ontology is

choices.text: a pattern of sequential organization
paramount truth value
self-expression
the "colonial gaze"
theoretical naivete

questions.prompt: The passage provides information that is most helpful in answering which one of the following questions?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
There's no way to pre-game *Five Questions*, so let's head to the answers and be willing to Ctrl + F or scan for where keywords in each answer choice are discussed in the passage. That way we can re-read what available text there is and see if a question gets answered.

We should observe that this question stem (atypically) is phrased in a *Most Supported* degree, "most helpful".

The normal wording of Five Questions is *Must Be True*:
"The passage provides information that is **sufficient** to answer which question"

So our 'answer' to the question might feel a little bit more loosely supported than normal.

choices.text: Why do the Kayapo use video technology to create legal records?
choices.explanation: Paragraph 4 says the Kayapo record transactions with Brazilian government representatives to provide legally binding records. It also identifies the Kayapo as primarily an oral society, which helps explain the use of recorded speech. The passage does not say they distrust written contracts or feel uncomfortable with writing; those additional attitudes are unnecessary speculation.

choices.text: What is the origin of the idea of the "noble savage"?
choices.explanation: The beginning of the 3rd paragraph alludes to an old-fashioned idea called the "noble savage", but we don't get any backstory on where it came from.

choices.text: Which indigenous cultures have not yet adopted Western video technologies?
choices.explanation:
The only named indigenous culture in the whole passage is the Kayapo, and they **have** adopted Western video technologies.

We wouldn't be able to answer this question then, since no other indigenous cultures were ever discussed in the passage.

choices.text: Which Western technologies entered cultural circulation in the fifteenth century?
choices.explanation: The beginning of the 3rd paragraph says that "no Western object that has entered cultural circulation since the 15th century has been neutral", but the passage provides no specific examples of any technology that actually entered circulation in the 15th century.

choices.text: What factors have made video equipment as inexpensive as it now is?
choices.tag: Unsupported Causal Relationship: why it's inexpensive
choices.explanation: The middle of the 1st paragraph says, "Because inexpensive video equipment is now available throughout the world ... ", but there is no causal backstory provided for why video equipment is available around the world at an inexpensive price.

questions.prompt: Terence Turner would be most likely to agree with which one of the following assessments of Weiner's position regarding the spread of video?

choices.text: Weiner fails to recognize the vast diversity of traditional practices among the world's indigenous peoples.
Weiner overestimates the extent to which video technology has become available throughout the world.
Weiner does not fully recognize the value of preserving the traditional practices of indigenous peoples.
Weiner underestimates indigenous peoples' capacity for adapting the products of alien cultures to fit their own cultural values.
Weiner ignores the fact that, even before the spread of video, many Western technologies had already been adapted by indigenous cultures.

questions.prompt: In using the phrase "technological determinism" (second sentence of the third paragraph), the author refers to the idea that

explanationBlocks.heading: Research
explanationBlocks.body:
This is the style of Meaning in Context that asks what a word / phrase **refers** to. The antecedent might be in the same paragraph, but it's common to have to look to preceding paragraphs.

When we try to match up "technological determinism" with its referent, we can first ask our brain, *what does determinism mean*?

It shows up in a lot of LSAT passages. Determinism means "a system in which stuff is determined / there's no free will / everything that happens is an inescapable result of other stuff that happened".

Technological determinism would probably either mean that "technology forces stuff to happen" or that "stuff forces technology to happen".

In the 2nd paragraph, Weiner said:
*video **technologies inevitably** purvey a Western ontology. Using video costs indigenous peoples the very cultural identity they seek to record.*

In the 3rd paragraph, we hear "technological determinism" used to refer to the idea that, "using a video camera makers one unwittingly Western".

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body:
So we know that "technological determinism" is a reference to what Weiner was saying in the middle of the 2nd paragraph.

It's the idea that by using Western technology (in the form of video cameras), it would necessarily lead to the Westernization of the indigenous peoples using the cameras.

choices.text: technology is exchanged in ways that appear to be predestined
choices.explanation:
This doesn't have anything to do with "indigenous people being forced to adopt Western values because they are using Western technology".

This is just an answer meant for people who don't research the context.

What does "technological determinism" refer to?
*technological* = technology
*determinism* = predestined

The 2nd paragraph was never talking about predestined exchanges of technology.

choices.text: the technologies used by field anthropologists influence their views of the cultures they study
choices.explanation:
We're looking for the idea that "when indigenous people use Western technology (like video cameras), it necessarily imparts Western cultural values on them".

This is talking about the anthropologists being influenced by the technologies they use, not about indigenous people being influenced by borrowing the Western technologies.

choices.text: cultures generally evolve in the direction of greater dependence on technology
choices.explanation:
Nothing in the 2nd paragraph was saying that *most* cultures evolve to have greater dependence on technology.

"Technological determinism" was the idea that if indigenous people use Western technology, then Western values will be imposed on them.

choices.text: a culture's ethical values determine its reaction to new technologies
choices.explanation:
We're looking for the idea that "using new technology changes a culture's values".

This is saying that "a culture's values affect its reaction to new technology." The culture's values shouldn't be the Cause in this idea. They are the Effect.

choices.text: cultures are shaped in fundamental ways by the technologies they use
choices.explanation:
This is our best match for the idea that "if indigenous people use Western technology (like cameras), then they will be changed by the Western values that come with that technology."

The technology is shaping/determining the culture, just as Weiner was worried about.

passages.title: Judicial Recusals
passages.text:
The current approach to recusal and disqualification of judges heavily emphasizes appearance-based analysis. Professional codes of conduct for judges typically focus on the avoidance of both impropriety and the appearance of impropriety. Judges are expected to recuse (i.e., remove) themselves from any case in which their impartiality might reasonably be questioned. In some jurisdictions, statutes allow a party to a court proceeding to request disqualification of a judge for bias. In other jurisdictions, the responsibility for recusal falls upon the judge alone.

The rules provide vague guidance at best, making disqualification dependent on whether the judge’s impartiality “might reasonably be questioned,” without giving any idea of whose perspective to take or how to interpret the facts. It is a mistake for rules governing judicial ethics to focus on the appearance of justice rather than on the elimination of bias that renders a judge cognitively incapable of properly reaching a just outcome because of a too-close personal involvement in the matter before the court. Focusing on appearances may cause sources of actual bias that are not apparent to outside observers, or even to judges themselves, to be overlooked.

The function of the law is the settlement of normative disputes. Such settlement will work only if it is well reasoned. The achievement of actual justice by the use of legal reasoning is the primary function of judges. Therefore, the best way to address concerns about judicial impartiality is to require judges to make their reasoning transparent. Accordingly, we should eliminate disqualification motions alleging bias, whether actual or apparent. This unreliable mechanism should be replaced by the requirement of a written explanation of either the reasons for a judge’s decision to recuse, or if the judge decides against recusal, the legal basis for the judgment reached, based on the merits of the case. That is, judges should not be required to explain why they did not recuse themselves, but rather they should be required to show the legal reasoning on the basis of which their ultimate judgments were made.

A potential objection is that the reasoning given by the judge, however legally adequate, may not be the judge’s real reasoning, thus allowing for the presence of undetected bias. However, as long as a knowledgeable observer cannot find any fault with the legal reasoning provided, then there are no grounds for complaint. Under the law, a right of recourse arises only if harm accrues. If a judge who had no improper considerations in mind could have reached the same conclusion for the reasons stated by a judge who had hidden reasons in mind, then there is no harm on which to base a complaint.

summaries.standard:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

Judicial recusal and disqualification: appearance of bias vs. addressing actual bias through judicial transparency.

**Framework**

Challenge Position (the author critiques the current appearance-focused approach and offers a different solution)

**Main Point**

Instead of focusing on the appearance of impropriety, judicial ethics rules should prioritize eliminating actual bias by requiring judges to make their legal reasoning transparent, rather than relying on disqualification motions or appearance-based standards.
**The Most Valuable Sentence appears in paragraph 2: "It is a mistake for rules governing judicial ethics to focus on the appearance of justice rather than on the elimination of bias that renders a judge cognitively incapable of properly reaching a just outcome because of a too-close personal involvement in the matter before the court."**

**P1: Current Approach – Focus on Appearances**

The passage starts by explaining that most codes and laws about judges stepping away from cases (recusal) are all about avoiding not just actual bias, but even the appearance of it. In some places, someone involved in a case can request a judge step down for bias, but in others, it's up to the judge to choose to recuse themself.

**P2: Critique of the Current System**

The author points out that these rules are vague and mostly worry about appearances of fairness, not actual bias. The author argues that's a mistake—focusing on appearances can miss real sources of bias that aren’t obvious to outsiders or even to judges themselves.

**P3: Author's Solution – Require Transparent Legal Reasoning**

Now the author argues for a better system: judges should be required to explain the legal reasoning behind their decisions, especially when they choose not to recuse themselves. Instead of filing motions about possible bias, focus should shift to whether the judge’s logic is solid and out in the open.

**P4: Addressing Potential Objections**

Some might object that a judge’s official explanation might hide their real (possibly biased) reasons. But the author says as long as the reasoning stands up to scrutiny, there’s no basis for complaints. Legally, unless there’s demonstrable harm, there’s no recourse—if the decision could have been reached without bias, then there’s nothing to object to.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, a weakness of current rules regarding recusal and disqualification is that they

choices.text: interfere with judges' reasoning about the cases that they hear
fail to specify whose perspective is relevant to determining apparent bias
exaggerate the importance of transparency in judicial reasoning
place responsibility for recusal entirely on judges
ignore the importance of the appearance of propriety

questions.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the primary purpose of the second paragraph?

choices.text: to state the author's objections to the approach described in the first paragraph
to present a solution that is rejected in the third paragraph
to provide concrete examples of the problems discussed in the first paragraph
to explore the history that led to the situation described in the first paragraph
to state the thesis to be defended in the rest of the passage

questions.prompt: The author of the passage regards the legal principle that "a right of recourse arises only if harm accrues" (second-to-last sentence of the passage) as

choices.text: an established principle of law
part of the definition of the function of the law
a tool for judges to disguise their real reasoning
unfair to parties to legal proceedings
central to the current means of addressing judicial bias

questions.prompt: It can be inferred from the passage that the author would be most likely to consider which one of the following to be a weakness of statutes that allow parties to court proceedings to request disqualification of judges for bias?

explanationBlocks.heading: Research
explanationBlocks.body:
The language of "statutes that allow parties to request disqualification" comes from the second to last sentence of the 1st paragraph.

Nothing in that sentence talks about "a weakness", though. The first paragraph is pretty neutral overall.

But we know that the author ultimately has a negative view towards the current way that recusals / disqualifications are done. Why?

- the rules are vague
- they rely on appearances (if the judge looks biased or someone might question whether the judge is biased, that's enough)
- the author thinks that this means that some unbiased judges will be forced to recuse just for the sake of appearing fair, and that some judges who *do* have a bias for a certain case will end up hearing that case anyway because no one knew to call them out on their potential bias.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body:
The author's gripe in the 2nd paragraph is that "focusing on appearances may cause sources of actual bias that are not apparent to outside observers, or even to judges themselves, to be overlooked".

So a weakness she would find with statutes that allow a party to a court proceeding to request disqualification could be that these parties might not be privy to source of actual bias. It might not be apparent to them as an outside observer. So they might allow a judge to sit for their trial, not knowing that the judge has some actual bias.

choices.text: The guidelines for applying such statutes are excessively rigid.
choices.explanation: The author calls the guidance vague: it does not identify the relevant perspective or explain how to interpret the facts. That is the stated defect. Vagueness and rigidity are not logical opposites in every possible rule system, but this passage does not establish excessive rigidity.

choices.text: Such statutes are incompatible with a requirement that judges make their reasoning transparent.
choices.explanation: The author recommends replacing disqualification motions with written reasoning. A recommendation to replace one mechanism does not establish that the mechanisms are logically incompatible or could never be used together.

choices.text: Such statutes can fail to eliminate actual bias because parties to court proceedings are not always aware of judges' prejudices.
choices.explanation:
This aligns with our available support text. The author doesn't identify any weaknesses or negative things in the 1st paragraph.

She talks about the weaknesses of the current system in the 2nd paragraph. The only part of the paragraph that seems to touch on the idea of "a party to a court proceeding" is that final sentence of the 2nd, which says:

*Focusing on appearances may cause sources of actual bias that are **not apparent to outside observers** to be overlooked.*

This matches well with this sentence. A party to a court proceeding is not always aware of sources of actual bias. They might overlook it and thus never have reason to request a disqualification of the judge, and thus fail to eliminate a judge with actual bias.

choices.text: Such statutes conflict with professional codes of conduct that require judges to recuse themselves if they believe that they are biased.
choices.explanation:
The author isn't ever saying that we either have judges recuse themselves, or we have parties to a court proceeding be allowed to request disqualifications. But **you can't have both**. They conflict.

The final sentence of the 1st paragraph contradicts the idea that these two things can't coexist.

We heard, "in some jurisdictions, a party to a court proceeding can request disqualification (or a judge can remove themselves). In other jurisdictions the responsibility falls upon the judge **alone**."

The use of "alone" implies that in the previous case, the judge was not alone in deciding whether or not to recuse themselves. They might decide to and/or a party to the court proceeding might request a disqualification. The responsibility for recusal is **shared** by judges and parties to proceedings.

choices.text: There is no guarantee that all requests for disqualification of judges will be granted.
choices.explanation:
The author never complains about giving parties to a proceeding to power to request disqualification of a judge for bias, **because it won't have a 100% success rate**.

That would be an insane complaint. "If this request process doesn't always result in requests being granted, then I don't like it." And we have no text to point to that sounds anything like that complaint.

questions.prompt: The passage suggests that if judges are required to provide written explanations for the legal reasoning underlying their decisions about cases, then

choices.text: judicial bias will be almost completely eliminated
any faulty reasoning employed by judges can in principle be detected
judges' written explanations will usually conceal their real reasoning
the public perception of the impartiality of the judiciary will improve
judges will be motivated to recuse themselves when there is an appearance of bias

questions.prompt: Which one of the following would be an example of the kind of "real reasoning" referred to in the first sentence of the last paragraph of the passage?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
Let’s think about how we would paraphrase this section of the text. The author is saying in the previous paragraph that judges should write an explanation of why they recused themselves, if they choose to recuse. If they don’t choose to recuse themselves, then they don’t need to explain *that* decision; but they *do* need to explain the reasoning they used to decide a case.

That way outsiders could see whether the case was decided on legitimate grounds, rather than on the biased preferences of the judge.

So in the beginning of the last paragraph, the author is thinking that someone might say, “Even if the judge *says* she acquitted the baker of tax fraud based it was never clearly established that he had any intent to deceive, she might ****really**** be acquitting him because she loves that store and wants some free cupcakes.”

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: Thus, the *real reasoning* refers to what was really in the judge’s heart as they decided the case, not the supposed rationale the judge wrote down.

choices.text: the reasoning leading to a judge's decision against recusal
choices.explanation: This answer concerns the reasoning behind a decision not to recuse. The target sentence instead concerns the real reasons for the ultimate judgment on the case, which may differ from the legally adequate reasons written in its explanation.

choices.text: an argument that is too technical to be understood by someone without formal legal training
choices.explanation: Being "overly technical" has nothing to do with what we’re looking for, which is “what was *really* in the judge’s mind/heart as she decided the case / the *true* / secret reason that she decided the way she did”.

choices.text: reasoning that is motivated by the judge's personal animus against a defendant
choices.explanation:
This sounds like an example of what we’re looking for, “what was *really* in the judge’s mind/heart as she decided the case; the *true* / *secret* reason that she decided the way she did”.

In this example the judge’s bias was based on hating the defendant. She might right a plausible legal rationale for why she found the defendant guilty, but her ****real reason**** for doing so was that she just hates this dude.

choices.text: reasoning that a knowledgeable observer cannot find any fault with
choices.explanation: The “fake” reason offered by the judge is the “reasoning a knowledgeable observer cannot find fault with”. The “real” reason is the one motivated by the judge’s bias. The judge wants to keep this real reasoning a secret, so this reasoning won’t be published, and if it were, a knowledgeable observer would definitely find fault with it.

choices.text: a central legal principle referred to in a judge's written explanation
choices.tag: Out of Scope: central legal principle
choices.explanation: This has nothing to do with what we’re looking for, which is “what was *really* in the judge’s mind/heart as she decided the case / the *true* / *secret* reason that she decided the way she did”.

questions.prompt: The author would be most likely to consider which one of the following to be an accurate description of the effects of the current approach to recusal and disqualification of judges?

explanationBlocks.heading: Research
explanationBlocks.body:
The first paragraph begins by talking about the current approach, so we need to read from there to see where the author discusses the **effects** of the current approach.

The 1st sentence tells us what it *emphasizes*. The 2nd tells us what judges are expected to do. The 3rd and 4th sentences discuss variations from region to region.

Okay, so no "effect" yet. We move on to the 2nd paragraph. The first sentence there provides an effect:

"The rules provide vague guidance, **making** disqualification dependent on whether judge's impartiality could be reasonably questioned."

The second sentence of the 2nd paragraph just provides our author's negative evaluation of this, but nothing causal.

Finally, the last sentence of the 2nd paragraph seems to give us the "effects":

*Focusing on appearances (as the current approach does) may cause sources of actual bias that are not apparent to outside observers, or even to judges themselves, to be overlooked*.

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body: Let's see if there's an answer that seems to play off the 1st or last sentence of the 2nd paragraph.

choices.text: The standards in place fail to assure the general public that the legal system is adequately protected against judicial bias.
choices.tag: Out of Scope: fail to assure public
choices.explanation:
This is a pretty tempting answer. "Failing to assure someone of X" is a pretty soft idea, because assuring someone of X is pretty strong.

We might keep this on a first pass, but ultimately the author isn't saying that the problem with the current approach is that it's failing to assure the general public that we're protecting against bias -- it's that we're not actually doing a good job protecting against bias.

Since the current approach "focuses on appearances", it is actually probably good at convincing people we're eliminating bias. The author isn't concerned that people are discouraged about the protections against bias.

The author is concerned that the current system might leave people feeling satisfied that we've protected against bias, while "sources of actual bias that are not apparent to outside observers (like the public) go overlooked".

choices.text: The professional codes of conduct for judges are considered meddlesome and ineffective by many judges.
choices.explanation:
We have no support for the notion that judges find their professional codes of conduct meddlesome or ineffective.

This has nothing to do with our Support Text at the end of the 2nd paragraph.

choices.text: Judges are rarely removed from cases for bias when they are not actually biased, but they are allowed to sit on many cases even though they are biased.
choices.explanation: The passage does not establish how often unbiased judges are removed or how many cases biased judges hear. It supports the weaker possibility that appearance-based rules remove some unbiased judges while missing some actual bias. A rate of removal among unbiased judges must not be reversed into a claim about how many removed judges are actually biased.

choices.text: Judges are rarely allowed to sit on cases when they are biased, but judges are removed from many cases for bias even though they are not actually biased.
choices.explanation: The passage does not quantify how often biased judges are allowed to sit or how many unbiased removals occur. It warns that actual bias can go unnoticed. Those limited claims support E without establishing the frequency claims in D.

choices.text: Judges are sometimes removed from cases for bias even though they are not actually biased, while some instances of judicial bias occur and are never detected.
choices.explanation:
This is instantly our most lovable answer on a first pass, because of the soft language: *sometimes / some instances*

The middle sentence of the 2nd paragraph suggests that judges are sometimes removed from cases because of the *appearance* of bias, even though their involvement in the case would not make them cognitively incapable of properly reaching a just outcome.

The final sentence of the 2nd paragraph suggests that an actual source of bias might be present but overlooked by outside observers and even judges themselves, and thus never detected.

passages.title: A Lie for a Lie
passages.text:
**Passage A**

Saint Augustine wrote that to proceed against lies by lying would be like countering robbery with robbery. To respond to wrongdoing by emulating it is certainly at times to accept lower standards.

And yet it has seemed to many that there is indeed some justification for repaying lies with lies. Such views go back as far as the kind of justice that demands an eye for an eye. They appeal to our sense of fairness: to lie to liars is to give them what they deserve, to restore an equilibrium they themselves have upset. Just as bullies forfeit the right not to be interfered with by others, so liars forfeit the right to be dealt with honestly.

Two separate moral questions are involved in this debate. The first asks whether a liar has the same claim to be told the truth as an honest person. The second asks whether one is more justified in lying to a liar than to others.

In order to see this distinction clearly, consider a person known by all to be a pathological liar but quite harmless. Surely, as the idea of forfeiture suggests, the liar would have no cause for complaint if lied to. But his tall tales would not constitute sufficient reason to lie to him. For the harm to self, others, and general trust that can come from the practice of lying has to be taken into account in weighing how to deal with him, not merely his personal characteristics.

**Passage B**

A view derived from Immanuel Kant holds that when rational beings act immorally toward others, then, by virtue of their status as rational beings, they implicitly authorize similar actions as punishment aimed toward themselves. That is, acting rationally, one always acts as one would have others act toward oneself. Consequently, to act toward a person as that person has acted toward others is to treat that person as a rational being, that is, as if that person’s act is the product of a rational decision.

From this it might be concluded that we have a duty to do to offenders what they have done, since this amounts to according them the respect due rational beings. But the assertion of a duty to punish seems excessive, since if this duty to others is necessary to accord them the respect due rational beings, then we would have a duty to do to all rational persons everything—good, bad, or indifferent—that they do to others. The point is rather that by your acts and by virtue of your status as a rational being, you authorize others to do the same to you; you do not compel them to do so. The Kantian argument leads to a right rather than a duty. Rational beings cannot validly object to being treated in the way in which they treated others. Where there is no valid complaint, there is no injustice, and where there is no injustice, others have acted within their rights.

summaries.standard:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

The moral justification (or lack thereof) for lying to liars, including distinctions between rights and duties as explored through Augustine and Kantian philosophy.

**Framework**

Present Debate

**Main Point**

The passages examine whether it is morally permissible (or even obligatory) to lie to liars, highlighting the distinction between viewing the act as a forfeiture of the right to honesty or creating a duty to repay lies with lies; ultimately, both passages challenge the idea that previous wrongdoing justifies counter-wrongdoing without qualification.
The Most Valuable Sentences:

- Passage A: "But his tall tales would not constitute sufficient reason to lie to him." (final paragraph)
- Passage B: "Rational beings cannot validly object to being treated in the way in which they treated others. Where there is no valid complaint, there is no injustice, and where there is no injustice, others have acted within their rights." (final paragraph)

**P1: Augustine’s View – Passing on Wrongdoing Is Not Justified (Passage A)**

Augustine argues that responding to lies by lying is as morally wrong as fighting robbery with robbery. It's a lowering of moral standards to meet the level of the wrongdoer.

**P2: Counterpoint – The Eye-for-an-Eye Appeal (Passage A)**

Still, many people feel it's fair to lie to liars—sort of a taste of their own medicine. There’s a sense of balance: just as bullies lose their right not to be pushed around, liars forfeit their right to honest treatment.

**P3: Clarifying the Moral Questions (Passage A)**

The author breaks the issue into two questions: Do liars have the same right to truth as honest people? Are we more justified in lying to liars than to others?

**P4: Distinction Between Right and Justification (Passage A)**

The author uses the example of a harmless, compulsive liar to show the distinction: while such a person may not have grounds to complain if lied to, that alone doesn’t make it right or justified to lie to them. We also have to consider the broader harm that comes from lying.

**P1: Kantian Perspective – Authorization Through Rational Action (Passage B)**

Kant’s philosophy says that when rational beings act wrongly toward others, they implicitly grant permission for others to act the same way toward them, because by acting rationally you’re saying, “This is how I think rational action should work.”

**P2: From Right to Duty – Limits of the Kantian View (Passage B)**

The passage considers whether this means we have a positive duty to repay wrongs in kind, but argues that’s too extreme. The more accurate reading: people authorize similar actions against themselves, but don’t require others to take those actions. It’s a forfeiture of complaint, not a moral obligation to retaliate.

**P3: Kantian Conclusion – Rights, Not Duties (Passage B)**

Ultimately, the Kantian view leads to the conclusion that there is a right (not a duty) to treat people as they have treated others, and if someone is treated as they have treated others, they cannot justifiably complain.

questions.prompt: Both passages are concerned with answering which one of the following questions?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
Passage A was grappling with the moral question of "should you lie to a liar?" We can probably eliminate a lot of answers just by seeing whether they would match up with A.

Passage B never talks about lying specifically, but it addresses the same underlying moral question of "should you reciprocate the wrong action that someone did to you?"

choices.text: Can immoral actions be harmless?
choices.tag: Fails B / Weak Match for A
choices.explanation:
"Harmless" is used in the beginning of A's final paragraph as a mere descriptor of a hypothetical pathological liar. The author wasn't trying to answer a question about harmlessness. She just posed a thought experiment and said, "Suppose this dude were harmless."

Passage B doesn't seem to ever address the question of whether immoral actions are sometimes harmless.

choices.text: Should the same rules apply in evaluating moral wrongs and criminal wrongs?
choices.explanation: Both passages are dealing only with interpersonal morality -- do we have moral rights to lie to liars. Neither passage ventures into criminal law.

choices.text: Is it right to respond to a person's wrongdoing with an action of the same kind?
choices.explanation: Passage A asks whether another person's lying provides sufficient justification for lying in return, taking wider harms into account. Passage B examines whether a rational wrongdoer authorizes corresponding treatment and distinguishes a right to respond from a duty. Both concern the moral status of responding in kind; neither must be read as imposing a duty to retaliate.

choices.text: What is the difference between a duty and a right?
choices.explanation:
While passage B displays an awareness of a distinction between duty and right, it never asks that question or provides an answer.

More importantly, passage A never brings up duty whatsoever.

choices.text: Is it just to treat all wrongdoers as rational beings?
choices.explanation:
While passage B definitely discusses Kant's notion that wrongdoers, ****if**** they are rational beings, are justly treated with the same wrongdoing they inflicted on us, passage B never addresses whether we should treat ****all**** wrongdoers as rational beings? (Even people who are mentally ill / even crimes of passion?)

More importantly, passage A never discusses the concept of rationality at all.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following considerations is introduced in passage A but not in passage B?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body: It's generally very hard to predict an answer to, "Which of these was in one passage but not the other", so we just head into the answers.

choices.text: the harm that may result as a consequence of treating people as they treat others
choices.explanation:
This comes from the final sentence of Passage A. The author is talking about whether or not we should lie to a pathological liar (treat him as he treated us), and she says even though he lies to us that doesn't necessarily give us good reason to lie to him.

After all, we need to take into account "the harm to self, others, and general trust that can come from the practice of lying".

Passage B talks about treating others as you've been treated in order to accord them respect as rational beings, but never talks about the harm of doing so.

choices.text: the consequences of not reciprocating another's wrongdoing
choices.tag: Opposite (if anything): More B than A
choices.explanation: Passage A discusses the harms of reciprocating a lie, not a distinct account of the consequences of declining to reciprocate. Do not infer that declining necessarily denies someone respect merely because responding in kind can accord respect. Passage B expressly distinguishes authorization from compulsion.

choices.text: the properties an action must have to count as rational
choices.tag: Opposite (if anything): More B than A
choices.explanation: Really, neither passage defines the necessary properties of a rational action, but given that passage B was the only passage discussing rationality at all, we can tell this wouldn't be the "A, but not B" idea we're looking for.

choices.text: the extent to which people who break moral rules are due respect
choices.explanation:
Passage B definitely talks about what respect is / isn't due to people who break moral rules. That's part of the whole discussion around "reciprocating how they treated you is showing them you think they are a rational being".

Passage B's second paragraph is specifically talking about "the respect due rational beings".

choices.text: instances in which people have been wronged by being treated as they treated others
choices.explanation: Neither passage brings up any instances / examples. Passage A has a thought experiment about a pathological liar, but the thought experiment doesn't count as an instance, nor does it include any description of someone actually lying to that liar (it's only a discussion of *should we / could we* lie to that liar).

questions.prompt: The passages are alike in that each seeks to advance its main argument by

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body: These questions that ask about each author's Method are very tough to guess ahead of time. The correct answers have usually focused on a tiny moment from each passage, not necessarily a big idea, so it's just better to see what the answers are offering and figure out with each one whether we could match it up to both.

choices.text: anticipating and refuting the most probable objections to a theory
choices.tag: Out of Scope: most probable objections
choices.explanation:
It's not clear in passage A that there's any theory at all. The author seems to just be offering her take on an age old moral question: *should you lie to a liar?*

She only really brings up opposing ideas in the beginning, in her 2nd paragraph, just to get the conversation rolling. But they aren't objections to her "theory". They are just a point of view that she plans to object to.

Passage B's second paragraph begins by anticipating a possible reaction to the Kantian argument in the first paragraph:
*From this it might be concluded that ...*

But not only can we not say that's an objection to the theory (it's just a possible takeaway), we also only know that "people ****might**** conclude X from this", not that "the most probable reaction to this is X".

choices.text: using an analogy to support its overall claim
choices.explanation: Passage A's first line contains an analogy relevant to its overall argument, but passage B never provides any analogy to support its overall claim that responding to wrongdoers with similar wrong behavior is something we're allowed to do, but not necessarily something we should be doing.

choices.text: focusing on a specific case to illustrate a generalization
choices.explanation: Passage A's thought experiment about a pathological liar could probably be construed as "a specific case to illustrate a generalization", but passage B doesn't have any specific cases at all.

choices.text: suggesting that a view can have unreasonable consequences
choices.explanation:
The view that "justice demands an eye for an eye" can have unreasonable consequences, according to passage A, because lying to a liar can bring "harm to self, others, and general trust".

It would be unreasonable to say I *should* lie to a liar if doing so had the unreasonable consequence of making life worse for me, others, and society.

In passage B, the second paragraph is all about shutting down a mistaken consequence people might infer from the views of Kant in the first paragraph:

*From this it might be concluded that we have a duty to reciprocate harm to offenders. But the assertion of a duty to punish seems excessive* (i.e. unreasonable).

choices.text: offering and defending a new definition for a commonly used term
choices.explanation: I'm not sure what new definition to a commonly used term is offered by either passage.

questions.prompt: The author of passage A would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?

choices.text: Maintaining a policy of reciprocating wrongdoing fails to accord rational beings the respect that they are due.
People have a duty to respond to even the morally neutral actions of others with actions of the same kind.
It can be unjustified to treat a person in a certain way even though that person has forfeited the right not to be treated in that way.
There is no circumstance in which there is sufficient reason to counter a wrong with a wrong of the same kind.
To restore moral equilibrium, justice will occasionally require that an innocent person forfeit the right to be treated in a certain way.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately characterizes the difference between the kind of right referred to in the last sentence of the second paragraph of passage A and the kind of right referred to in the third-to-last sentence of passage B?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
In the 2nd paragraph of A, the use of right is that,
*when someone bullies, they* *****forfeit the right***** *not to be interfered with by others.*

What are some equivalent expressions we could say for that usage?
People generally have the right not to be bullied ...There is an ****moral expectation**** that people shouldn't bully them ... They're ****entitled**** to not be bullied.

In the final paragraph of B, it's saying that when you've done bad thing X, people have *a right, not a duty* to do bad thing X to you too.

They have the *prerogative,* the *privilege* to lie to you if you've lied to them. They're not obligated to, but they have a moral "get out of jail free" card if they happen to treat you the same bad way you treated them.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body:
How are they different?

Well, in the first case, it was talking about someone's right to ****not**** be bullied or lied to by someone else.

In the second case, it's talking about someone's right ****to**** bully or lie to someone else.

Chronologically, the first right comes before the second right. We all have a right to not be bullied by Jasper, but once Jasper bullies us, we now have a right (but not a duty) to bully Jasper.

choices.text: In passage A, the kind of right referred to is a legal right, whereas in passage B the kind of right referred to is a moral right.
choices.explanation:
Both passages are speaking about rights, more in the moral sense than in the legal sense.

The first right you have morally prohibits everyone else from doing bad thing X to you.

The second right you have is your moral permission to do X to do someone else (someone who's done X to you).

choices.text: In passage A, the kind of right referred to involves benefits granted by society, whereas in passage B the kind of right referred to involves benefits granted by an individual in a position of authority.
choices.tag: Out of Scope: position of authority
choices.explanation:
Neither one is talking about a right invested by a position of authority, like a leader of state or a constitution.

They're both talking about moral rights to which we're all entitled.

choices.text: In passage A, the kind of right referred to is an entitlement held by groups of people, whereas in passage B the kind of right referred to is an entitlement held only by individuals.
choices.explanation: The right not to be bullied as well as the right to bully someone who's bullied you are both *individual* rights.

choices.text: In passage A, the kind of right referred to is something that cannot be given up, whereas in passage B the kind of right referred to is something that can be lost because of certain actions.
choices.explanation:
The reference to *right* in passage A is actually saying that someone *forfeits* (gives up) the right in certain circumstances.

So we know that passage A would not say it's a right that cannot be given up.

choices.text: In passage A, the kind of right referred to involves behavior that one is entitled to from others, whereas in passage B the kind of right referred to involves behavior that one is licensed to engage in.
choices.explanation:
*The right not to be bullied* is referring to behavior you're entitled to from others. Others aren't allowed to bully you. You're entitled to more respectful behavior.

*The right, but not the duty, to do to offenders what they have done* involves our ability to behave towards them in a way we wouldn't ordinarily be entitled to. We aren't usually licensed to engage in lying or bullying, but we have the right to do so to someone who has lied to or bullied us.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, would most help to make the suggestion in passage A that a harmless pathological liar's tall tales would not constitute sufficient reason to lie to him (second-to-last sentence of passage A) compatible with the Kantian argument laid out in the first paragraph of passage B?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body: The question asks about a specific case: the harmless pathological liar in A, and the Kantian argument in B's first paragraph. A says those tall tales do not supply sufficient reason to lie in return. B's argument concerns immoral acts that are products of rational decisions. A new fact excluding pathological behavior from rational action would keep this liar outside the condition on which that argument relies. A request to reconcile ideas does not prove a formal contradiction, and we should not invent a duty that B later explicitly rejects.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: Look for a fact that limits the rational-action argument's application to this pathological liar, allowing both positions to stand.

choices.text: Responding to pathological behavior with pathological behavior is irrational.
choices.explanation: The issue is whether the pathological liar's own act falls under B's rational-action argument. Saying that responding pathologically is irrational does not address that condition; an ordinary retaliatory lie also need not itself be compulsive pathological behavior.

choices.text: Rationality cannot be reasonably attributed to pathological behavior.
choices.explanation: B's argument depends on regarding the wrongdoer's act as a rational decision. If rationality cannot reasonably be attributed to pathological behavior, this liar's tall tales do not activate that argument. A can therefore deny that the tales supply sufficient reason to lie without contradicting the argument about rational wrongdoers. This reconciliation does not require a duty to retaliate.

choices.text: Pathological liars, if harmless, deserve to be treated as rational beings by others.
choices.explanation: This does not exclude the pathological case from the rational-agent rationale. Instead it preserves the condition under which B connects responding in kind with respect for rational agency, leaving the specific tension with A unresolved.

choices.text: Having the right to lie to a pathological liar is not equivalent to having a duty to do so.
choices.tag: Does Not Resolve the Specific Case
choices.explanation: The right-duty distinction is discussed later in B, but this question specifically compares A's pathological case with the argument in B's first paragraph. Absence of a duty does not by itself explain why that first-paragraph rationale supplies no sufficient reason in this case. B directly addresses the relevant condition by denying rationality to pathological behavior.

choices.text: To model one's behavior on that of a pathological liar is to lower one's own standards.
choices.tag: Does Not Resolve the Specific Case
choices.explanation: This adds a reason for avoiding imitation of the liar but does not explain how that reason fits the first-paragraph argument about rational agency. B makes the positions compatible by excluding pathological behavior from that argument's rational-action condition.

passages.title: The Myth of Liquid Glass
passages.text:
To glass researchers it seems somewhat strange that many people throughout the world share the persistent belief that window glass flows slowly downward like a very viscous liquid. Repeated in reference books, in science classes, and elsewhere, the idea has often been invoked to explain ripply windows in old houses. The origins of the myth are unclear, but the confusion probably arose partly from a misunderstanding of the fact that the atoms in glass are not arranged in a fixed crystal structure. In this respect, the structure of liquid glass and the structure of solid glass are very similar, but thermodynamically they are not the same. Glass does not have a precise freezing point; rather, it has what is known as a glass transition temperature, typically a range of a few hundred degrees Celsius. Cooled below the lower end of this range, molten glass retains an amorphous atomic structure, but it takes on the physical properties of a solid.

However, a new study debunks the persistent belief that stained glass windows in medieval cathedrals are noticeably thicker at the bottom because the glass flows downward. Under the force of gravity, certain solid materials including glass can, in fact, flow slightly. But Brazilian researcher Edgar Dutra Zanotto has calculated the time needed for viscous flow to change the thickness of different types of glass by a noticeable amount, and, according to his calculations, medieval cathedral glass would require a period well beyond the age of the universe.

The chemical composition of the glass determines the rate of flow. Even germanium oxide glass, which flows more easily than other types, would take many trillions of years to sag noticeably, Zanotto calculates. Medieval stained glass contains impurities that could lower the viscosity and speed the flow to some degree, but even a significant difference in this regard would not alter the conclusion, since the cathedrals are only several hundred years old. The study demonstrates dramatically what many scientists had reasoned earlier based on information such as the fact that for glass to have more than a negligible ability to flow, it would have to be heated to at least 350 degrees Celsius.

The difference in thickness sometimes observed in antique windows probably results instead from glass manufacturing methods. Until the nineteenth century, the only way to make window glass was to blow molten glass into a large globe and then flatten it into a disk. Whirling the disk introduced ripples and thickened the edges. To achieve structural stability, it would have made sense to install these panes in such a way that the thick portions were at the bottom. Later, glass was drawn into sheets by pulling it from the melt on a rod, a method that made windows more uniform. Today, most window glass is made by floating liquid glass on molten tin. This process makes the surface extremely flat.

summaries.standard:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

The myth that old window glass flows downward over time, and the science debunking it.

**Framework**

Challenge Position

**Main Point**

The commonly held belief that window glass flows downward over time (causing old windows to be thicker at the bottom) is a myth; scientific calculations and historical glassmaking techniques explain the thickness differences instead. (The main point is most directly addressed at the beginning of paragraph 2 and fully explained in the last paragraph.)

**P1: Introduction to the Glass Flow Myth**

A lot of people (even in science books) mistakenly believe that window glass is a super slow-moving liquid and gradually flows downward, explaining the thicker bottoms in old windows. This myth likely started because glass's atoms are not arranged like in crystals, but the structure alone doesn't mean glass is liquid—it's solid at room temperature, just with a unique atomic arrangement.

**P2: Scientific Debunking**

A recent study shows that, although glass *can* flow under gravity, it would take longer than the age of the universe for old windows to change thickness from flow. So, that's not the reason old windows are thicker at the bottom!

**P3: Why Flow Still Isn’t the Answer**

Even the easiest-flowing glass (like germanium oxide glass) would still take trillions of years to change shape noticeably, and medieval glass—even with impurities—wouldn't flow in just a few centuries. The science is clear: for glass to have more than a negligible ability to flow, it would need to be heated to at least 350°C.

**P4: Real Explanation—Old Glassmaking Techniques**

Those thicker, rippled old windows are because of how glass was made before modern methods—not because of flow. Old glass was blown, spun, and flattened, which left thicker edges, and it made sense to install panes with the thick part at the bottom. Later techniques produced more even panes, and today’s glass is super-flat thanks to floating it on molten tin.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
The central topic of the passage is whether glass flows slowly down like a viscous liquid.

Why is the author writing about this? What framework did we use?

The author wants to *Clarify a Misconception*. People persistently believe this myth about glass flowing slowly downward, and the author is presenting Zanotto's study which debunks this myth.

It's tough to settle on one Framework. In the sense that the author is trying to clarify a common misconception, it feels like *Challenge Position*. In the sense that two of the four paragraphs are focused on this **new** study, we might otherwise consider *Old / New* (the old belief being the popular misconception, the new belief being the debunking done by Zanotto).

However, the last paragraph introduces another possible framework: *Answer a Question*. In the last paragraph the author is saying, "So, the reason glass bulges at the bottom of old windows *isn't* because glass flows downward; it's because of old glass-making techniques.

Ultimately, we can probably roll these together into something like, "As Zanotto's new study shows, glass does not perceptibly flow downward over time, so the reason old windows bulge at the bottom is really just because of old glass-making techniques."

choices.text: Zanotto's research has proven that the amount of time required for viscous flow to change the thickness of medieval cathedral glass would be greater than the age of the universe.
choices.explanation:
This is a derivable claim from the end of the 2nd paragraph, but it doesn't have any of the big picture framing ideas.

Where's the *Challenge Position* part? It doesn't address the popular belief that glass flows downward.

Where's the *Answer a Question* part? It doesn't address the *real* reason that medieval cathedral glass bulges at the bottom (old glass-making techniques).

choices.text: The technology of window-glass production has progressed substantially from medieval stained-glass techniques to today's production of very flat and very uniform panes.
choices.explanation:
This answer's main clause is, "The technology of window-glass production has progressed substantially".

Did the author write this passage to update the world on window-glass production technology?

Heavens, no. She wrote it to go after the misconception that glass flows downward. The author was helping people let go of their misconception by telling them the *real* reason that old glass bulges at the bottom is because of the old school janky technology.

choices.text: After years of investigation motivated partly by a common misunderstanding about the structure of glass, scientists have developed ways of precisely calculating even extremely slow rates of gravity-induced flow in solids such as glass.
choices.explanation:
The main clause here is, "Scientists have developed ways of precisely calculating even slow rates of flow in solids such as glass".

Did the author write this passage in order to alert the world that science has gotten better at calculating the flow rates of solids?

Heck no. She wrote it to address the misconception that glass flows downward, to present a study debunking that idea, and to supply the real causal story behind the misconception.

The phrase "such as glass" in this answer makes it seem like glass was just one of potentially many examples of solids we were considering. Meanwhile, we know that glass wasn't an aside or an example. It was the central topic of the whole passage.

choices.text: Recent research provides evidence that although solid glass flows slightly under the influence of gravity, such flow is only one of several factors that have contributed to noticeable differences in thickness between the top and the bottom of some old windows.
choices.explanation:
This answer is conceding that solid glass *does* flow slightly downward. That flow *is* part of why there is a noticeable difference in thickness between the top and bottom of old windows.

This answer choice makes the passage out to be saying, "People think that old glass is thicker at the bottom because glass flows downward, and while that's true, there are other factors that also contribute."

The passage is actually saying, "People think old glass is thicker at the bottom because glass flows downward, but they're believing a myth. Scientists think it's weird how people insist on believing this. Luckily, a new study empirically debunks this myth. It would take trillions of years for the flow of glass to make any noticeable change in thickness, and these old windows are less than 1,000 years old."

The last sentence begins, "The difference in thickness in antique windows probably **results instead** from glass manufacturing methods". This answer is acting like it said, "... probably results **in addition** from glass manufacturing methods".

choices.text: Contrary to a commonly held belief, noticeable differences in thickness between the top and the bottom of some old glass windows are not due to the flowing of solid glass, but probably result instead from old glassworking techniques.
choices.explanation:
The main clause here is the *Challenge Position* part of the passage: **differences in thickness are not due to the flowing of solid glass.**

The final clause captures the *Answer a Question* final paragraph: **the real reason for old glass's weird thickness is glass manufacturing methods**.

questions.prompt: The passage most helps to answer which one of the following questions?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
There's no way to pre-game Five Questions, so let's head to the answers and use CTRL+F or our eyes to see where keywords in the answer choices appear in the passage, so that we can check to see whether the passage provides an answer.

We want to notice that this question stem is the squishier *Most Supported* version of Five Questions. It says the passage would "most help" to answer one of these questions (not the more *Must Be True* wording that the passage provides information "sufficient" to answer one of the questions).

choices.text: What is one way in which seventeenth-century windowpane manufacturing techniques differ from those commonly used in medieval times?
choices.explanation:
If we do a quick search/scan for 17th century, we'll see it's never mentioned in the passage.

The change in windowpane manufacturing techniques that is discussed in the last paragraph is a difference between medieval windows and 19th century windows.

choices.text: What is one way in which nineteenth-century windowpane manufacturing techniques differ from those commonly used today?
choices.explanation:
The last paragraph says that up until the 19th century they blow molten glass into a large globe and then flattened it.

Then we see "Later, glass was drawn into sheets by pulling it from the melt on a rod", which we can infer was the method used in the 19th century.

Whereas "**today**, most window glass is made by floating liquid glass on molten tin".

So that's the one way we know that 19th century techniques differ from those *commonly used* (i.e. "most window glass") today.

choices.text: Was glass ever used in windows prior to medieval times?
choices.explanation:
The passage talks about glass in medieval cathedrals, but it never talks about glass in any era prior to medieval times.

So we have no way of knowing from the passage whether glass was first used in medieval times or whether it predated medieval times.

choices.text: Are unevenly thick stained-glass windowpanes ever made of germanium oxide glass?
choices.explanation: We can find "germanium oxide" mentioned once, in the 3rd paragraph, and nothing in that sentence or the surrounding context reveals whether or not any unevenly thick stained-glass windowpanes are made of that type of glass.

choices.text: How did there come to be impurities in medieval stained glass?
choices.explanation:
"Impurities" are discussed in the sentence following the one about germanium oxide (3rd paragraph).

We're just told that medieval glass contained impurities. We don't know the backstory of how those impurities got there.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following best summarizes the author's view of the results of Zanotto's study?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
Zanotto's study is discussed in the 2nd and 3rd paragraphs. Can we find any author's attitude moments in there?

The first sentence of the 2nd paragraph says, "*a new study* ****debunks**** the persistent belief that glass windows bulge at the bottom because glass flows downward".

And the final sentence of the 3rd paragraph says, "*The study* ****demonstrates dramatically**** what many scientists had reasoned earlier based on information such as glass would need to be heated to at least 350º Celsius in order to have more than a negligible ability to flow.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: So let's look for an answer saying the author's view of the study is that it debunks the myth about flowing glass, or dramatically demonstrates what scientists had reasoned earlier.

choices.text: They provide some important quantitative data to support a view that was already held by many scientists.
choices.explanation:
We can match this up with the last sentence of the 3rd, in which the author says that Zanotto's study dramatically demonstrates what many scientists had reasoned earlier.

That sentence doesn't mention quantitative data, but can we support the notion that Zanotto provides important quantitative data?

Sure. The end of the 2nd and beginning of the 3rd paragraphs discuss Zanotto's study and both of those sentences talk about his calculations.

He calculated the time needed for viscous flow to change the thickness of different types of glass by a noticeable amount (many trillions of years at a minimum).

choices.text: They have stimulated important new research regarding an issue that scientists previously thought had been settled.
choices.tag: Out of Scope: stimulated new research
choices.explanation: Nothing in the 2nd or 3rd paragraphs talks about new research being stimulated by Zanotto.

choices.text: They offer a highly plausible explanation of how a mistaken hypothesis came to be widely believed.
choices.tag: Out of Scope: backstory of myth
choices.explanation:
This is saying that Zanotto's study tells us the story of how people came to mistakenly believe that glass flows downward.

But there's no support for that. From what we're told, all Zanotto's study does it provide calculations that show that people's belief that glass flows downward is false.

He debunks their belief; he doesn't explain the origin story of their belief.

choices.text: They provide a conceptual basis for reconciling two scientific views that were previously thought to be incompatible.
choices.explanation: There's nothing in the 2nd and 3rd paragraphs that's talking about reconciling scientific views. Is there *anything* in the passage about two scientific views that were previously thought to be incompatible (i.e. contradicting each other)?

choices.text: They suggest that neither of two hypotheses adequately explains a puzzling phenomenon.
choices.explanation:
The puzzling phenomenon was "why is the glass in old houses ripply? why do stained glass windows in medieval cathedrals get thicker at the bottom?"

There is only one hypothesis being considered at this point in the passage: glass flows downward over time, since its atoms are not in a fixed crystal structure.

Zanotto's study definitely suggests that "glass flows downward" is not an adequate explanation for the puzzling phenomenon (we could say even that it's an incredibly wrongheaded explanation).

But there isn't any ****second**** hypothesis that his research is undermining.

questions.prompt: The passage suggests that the atomic structure of glass is such that glass will

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body: Paragraph 1 distinguishes atomic arrangement from physical behavior. Glass retains an amorphous atomic structure as it cools through a transition range, yet below that range it has the physical properties of a solid. The passage uses transition temperature for a range, not a precise freezing point. Paragraphs 2 and 3 add that solid glass can flow slightly, while appreciable flow requires substantial heating. Keep the distinctions between atomic structure, temperature range and noticeable flow separate.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: Test each claim against those distinctions. Heating can change flow behavior without requiring a fixed crystalline arrangement.

choices.text: behave as a liquid even though it has certain properties of solids
choices.explanation:
The last sentence of the 1st paragraph is saying that solid glass "takes on the physical properties of a solid", which means "how the object behaves".

I can knock on solid glass, just like I'm knocking on the wall. It behaves like a solid. My knuckles have no idea that the glass's atomic structure is actually very similar to that of liquid glass.

choices.text: be noticeably deformed by the force of its own weight over a period of a few millennia
choices.explanation:
This language about being deformed by its own weight isn't coming from where we looked at the end of the 1st paragraph, but if we consider it, it seems to deal more with the 2nd paragraph's concerns.

The author thinks that Zanotto has ****debunked**** the idea that gravity will cause glass to sag downward until the bottom is thicker than the top (noticeably deformed).

Zanotto has calculated that *"the time needed for flow of glass to change by a noticeable amount is well more than the age of the universe*", let alone a period of a few millenia.

choices.text: behave as a solid even when it has reached its glass transition temperature
choices.explanation: The passage guarantees solid physical properties below the lower end of the transition range. It does not guarantee the same behavior after glass has been heated to that range. The phrase even when does not, by itself, mean always under every condition; the problem is the unsupported extension of solid behavior.

choices.text: flow downward under its own weight if it is heated to its glass transition temperature
choices.explanation: The passage presents glass as retaining an amorphous structure while its physical properties change across the transition range. Together with the account of gravity-induced flow and the need for substantial heating for non-negligible flow, this supports downward flow when glass is heated to its transition range.
