Do not treat this as a general rule that every conditional can be reversed.

choices.text: stop flowing only if the atoms are arranged in a fixed crystalline structure
choices.explanation: Paragraph 1 says glass can take on solid physical properties while remaining amorphous. A fixed crystalline arrangement is therefore not established as necessary for solid behavior. The answer adds an unsupported only-if requirement.

questions.prompt: The author of the passage attributes the belief that window glass flows noticeably downward over time to the erroneous assumption that

explanationBlocks.heading: Research
explanationBlocks.body:
In the first sentence of the passage it says that people believe that window glass flows slowly downward like a very viscous liquid.

Why?

*The origins of the myth are unclear, but the confusion probably arose partly from a misunderstanding of the fact that the atoms in glass are not arranged in a fixed crystal structure.*

Okay, that takes a bit to unpack:
- it's a fact that the atoms in glass are not arranged in a fixed crystal structure
- people misunderstand that fact
- and because of that they are confused into thinking that glass flows downward like a very viscous liquid.

How would a person look at the fact that "atoms in glass are not arranged in a fixed crystal structure" and get to the idea that "glass flows downward like a liquid"?

They must be assuming, "If it's not a fixed structure, then it's loose like a liquid and would flow downward".

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body: Let's look for something like "things without fixed structure will flow downward like a thick liquid".

choices.text: the atomic structure of solid glass is crystalline rather than amorphous
choices.explanation:
The author doesn't think that people assume that solid glass's atomic structure is crystalline (which would be a synonym for fixed structure).

She's explicitly saying they know that glass has a non-fixed structure (an amorphous one), and they misunderstand the significance of having a non-fixed structure (they think that means that it will flow like a thick liquid, but apparently it doesn't mean that).

choices.text: the amorphous atomic structure of glass causes it to behave like a very viscous liquid even in its solid form
choices.explanation:
We were looking for "If it's not a fixed crystal structure, then it will flow downward like a thick liquid", and that's basically what this is saying.

The amorphous (i.e. not-fixed into one shape) structure of the atoms means that it will behave like a viscous liquid.

"Glass" is presumed to be solid. So the persistent belief that "window glass (definitely considered a solid) flows slowly downward" tells us that people are thinking this downward flow occurs even in glass's solid form.

choices.text: methods of glass making in medieval times were similar to the methods used in modem times
choices.explanation: The proposed source of confusion is a misunderstanding of glass's noncrystalline atomic structure, not an assumption that medieval and modern manufacturing methods were similar.

choices.text: the transition temperature of the glass used in medieval windows is the same as that of the glass used in modem windows
choices.explanation: The author connects the misconception with the noncrystalline atomic structure of glass. Nothing attributes it to an assumption that medieval and modern transition temperatures match.

choices.text: liquid glass and solid glass are thermodynamically dissimilar
choices.explanation:
The author tells us that liquid glass and solid glass are **not** thermodynamically similar, as a way to set the record straight:

*Hey, everybody. Glass does **not** flow downward like a thick liquid. You're right that solid glass doesn't have a fixed crystal structure, so the structure of liquid and solid glass are similar. **But** ... (you're wrong to think solid glass flows like a liquid) because thermodynamically liquid and solid glass are not the same.*

So the people who think that solid glass does flow like a liquid would be more likely to think that solid and liquid glass are thermodynamically *similar*.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following is most analogous to the persistent belief about glass described in the passage?

choices.text: Most people believe that the tendency of certain fabrics to become wrinkled cannot be corrected during the manufacturing process.
Most people believe that certain flaws in early pottery were caused by the material used rather than the process used in manufacturing the pottery.
Most people believe that inadequate knowledge of manufacturing techniques shortens the life span of major appliances.
Most people believe that modern furniture made on an assembly line is inferior to individually crafted furniture.
Most people believe that modern buildings are able to withstand earthquakes because they are made from more durable materials than were older buildings.

questions.prompt: The passage suggests that which one of the following statements accurately characterizes the transition temperature of glass?

explanationBlocks.heading: Research
explanationBlocks.body:
We hear about the glass transition temperature in the 1st paragraph:

*Glass doesn't have a precise freezing point; rather it has what is known as a glass transition temperature, typically a range of a few hundred degrees Celsius. Cooled below the lower end of this range, liquid (molten) glass will retain an amorphous atomic structure but take on the physical properties of a solid.*

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: Nowhere else in the passage do we hear about the **glass transition temperature**, so we would potentially just read this snippet of text and then head to the answers thinking, "Which answer can I best support from the passage, leaning on what I'm told in these two sentences?"

choices.text: It is higher for medieval glass than for modern glass.
choices.explanation: The passage describes impurities in medieval glass and differences in manufacturing methods, but gives no comparison of medieval and modern transition temperatures. Neither the relative amount of impurities nor its effect on transition temperature is established here.

choices.text: It has only recently been calculated with precision.
choices.tag: Out of Scope: calculating transition temp
choices.explanation:
The recent calculations in this passage all come from Zanotto, and he never calculates a glass transition temperature.

He is calculating how long it would take for the viscous flow of glass to result in any noticeable lump at the bottom of the glass.

He calculated the "flow rate" of different types of glass, but didn't come up with some precise calculation of the glass transition temperature (the range through which a glass goes from being liquid to being pretty much solid).

choices.text: Its upper extreme is well above 350 degrees Celsius.
choices.explanation: Combine the transition range of a few hundred degrees in paragraph 1 with the statement in paragraph 3 that more than negligible flow requires heating to at least 350 degrees Celsius. In that account, 350 is a lower threshold for appreciable flow, rather than the upper end of the transition range. This supports an upper extreme well above it. The passage does not supply exact endpoints such as 300-600 degrees, and none should be invented.

choices.text: It does not affect the tendency of some kinds of glass to flow downward.
choices.explanation:
This answer is saying, "Some kinds of glass flow downward, and it has nothing to do with their glass transition temperature".

But since glass transition temperature refers to the temperature range through which glass goes from being a solid that doesn't flow to being something more liquid-y that does flow, the glass transition temperature is definitely related to whether or not a given type of glass (at a given temperature) would or wouldn't have any tendency to flow downward.

choices.text: For some types of glass, it is a specific temperature well below 350 degrees Celsius.
choices.explanation:
The transition temperature is never a **specific** singular temperature; glass doesn't have a **precise** freezing / melting point.

It's a range, usually, of a few hundred degrees Celsius.
